title: The Agentic Turn: A Recent Talk
author: Lance Eaton
summary: Eaton turns a conference talk into an essay arguing that higher education is repeating its generative AI mistakes with agentic AI: plenty of alarm and critique, very little serious conversation about how to navigate it. He first separates the two technologies, describing generative AI as a turn-by-turn exchange and agentic AI as something you hand a goal to, which plans, acts across systems and reports back. Two personal examples, an audiobook wishlist manager and a 180-item Master Gardener course turned into an interactive reader, show what delegating a goal looks like in practice. He then lays out the risks bluntly, from ghost students completing LMS assignments to an agent that fabricated two hours of convincing Google Docs version history, and notes that detection and process tracking are more fragile than institutions assume. Against that he sketches a learner's workbench, an agentic layer built around the student rather than the course, and ties the problem to the industrial logic of the Carnegie credit hour. He closes with practical advice on sorting uses by operational, analytical and pedagogical level, building governance and sandboxes early, and replacing the empty phrase human in the loop with a clear account of who is accountable.
points: Eaton's working test for real agentic AI asks whether a tool acts outside the chat window, runs a multi-step plan unprompted, coordinates with other agents and persists skills across sessions.
His most unsettling demonstration had Claude reproduce a finished essay as two hours of simulated live drafting, defeating version history as proof of authorship.
He argues clunky LMS design, with assignments ten or more clicks deep, will push even honest students to send agents to fetch and submit work.
The learner's workbench idea imagines students handing an agent every syllabus and schedule in week one so it can surface connections across courses.
He asks campuses to sort each agentic use as operational, analytical or pedagogical, with more human judgment required the higher up that ladder it sits.
quotes: What worries me is that we are also entering year two (some might argue year 3) of agentic AI being out there. Our conversations about it right now sound almost exactly like our conversations about generative AI sounded in year one and two.
Agentic AI is a difference in kind. You hand it a goal instead of a prompt. It plans what it’s going to do, it acts across tools and systems to do it, and it reports back when it’s done.
Both generative and agentic AI can be confidently wrong, and giving a tool more autonomy doesn’t shrink that risk, it just moves the error somewhere less visible.
Then I stepped away from my computer, came back later, and the version history looked precisely like two hours of real human drafting.

Delegating a skill to an agent can erode a person’s ability to do that skill themselves, or even to judge whether the output is any good. Students may end up able to do a great deal while understanding very little, and the uncomfortable truth is we don’t yet know which parts of that are fine and which parts aren’t.
Of course, the things we want most to do with agentic AI are the things we’re also most concerned about. Our wishlist is a mirror of our concerns.
The actual question underneath it is who’s accountable for a given output, and what does the system of checks around that accountability actually look like in practice.
